flavorText: An institutional heavy metal desk. The drawers have been welded shut to prevent hoarding.
There are faint scratch marks near the welded seams. Someone desperately tried to get inside.
The metal is cold. Whatever was in those drawers is long gone.
A sterile medical-grade vinyl chair. The upholstery squeaks faintly against the ambient hum of the facility.
There are deep indentations in the cushion, suggesting someone sat here for days on end without moving.
A faint serial number is stamped on the back leg: DEPT-COG-ALGN-004.
A brutalist concrete planter. The soil is completely dry and smells faintly of ozone.
Digging a finger into the dirt reveals a hard, metallic surface an inch below. Not a real planter.
The synthetic plant leaves are covered in a thin layer of grey dust.
A framed structural blueprint of the facility. The architecture seems mathematically impossible.
Tracing the lines reveals that the hallways fold back on themselves in an endless, recursive loop.
There are no exits marked anywhere on this document.
A thick glass isolation bell jar. Whatever was kept inside has already been removed.
The glass is lined with microscopic lead-lattice, used for containing highly volatile cognitive anomalies.
Looking closely at the base... the seal wasn't broken from the outside. Something pushed its way out.
The central frequency distillation unit. It requires precise acoustic calibration.
Its casing is lined with barium shielding. The Department used these to extract memories via sound.
A faint vibration pulses through the metal. It is actively waiting for an input frequency.
A machined brass cipher key resting on the desk surface.
Its teeth are cut in an irregular harmonic pattern designed to match the observation corridor tumbler.
The brass is cool to the touch and stamped with 'DEPT-COG-ALGN'.
A heavy classified clinical dossier folder. 'FORM 104-ALPHA // DEPT. OF COGNITIVE ALIGNMENT' is embossed on the front cover.
The wax seal is stamped with an insignia of a tuning fork striking a human skull.
It feels unusually heavy, as if the paper inside is lined with lead.
A heavy bakelite rotary telephone. The line is dead, but it still hums faintly.
The rotary dial is locked in place. You can only receive calls on this device, not make them.
Putting your ear to the receiver, you don't hear a dial tone. You hear rhythmic breathing.
A machined brass electrical shunt. It feels dense and cold to the touch.
There are deep scorch marks around the primary terminals. It must have bridged a massive electrical load.
Engraved along the side: 'CAUTION - COGNITIVE OVERLOAD PROTOCOL ONLY'.
A solid reinforced steel blast door. It seals the Sterile Chamber from the rest of the facility.
There are no handles or keyholes on this side. It is electronically magnetically locked.
The pneumatic seals are engaged. You are completely isolated.
Cold, seamless terrazzo flooring. It has been polished to a mirror finish.
There are faint circular scuff marks near the center of the room. Someone was pacing here for days.
The floor is completely impermeable. Even harsh chemicals can be hosed right off.
Standard-issue clinical green ceramic tiles. They cover the lower half of the walls.
The grout between the tiles is meticulously clean. Too clean.
Staring at the geometric grid of tiles for too long makes your eyes hurt.
A harsh, chalk-white plaster wall. It reflects the fluorescent light perfectly.
If you look closely at a grazing angle, there are faint, washed-out stains.
The walls are thick. You cannot hear a single sound from the outside world.
A massive two-way observation mirror. The room next door is pitch black.
The glass is heavily reinforced bulletproof acrylic. They were afraid of what you might do.
You can't see them, but you can feel them watching you from the dark.
A recessed fluorescent luminaire. It emits a harsh, shadowless white light.
The hum of the ballast matches the exact frequency of your developing headache.
It never turns off. There is no concept of day or night in the Sterile Chamber.
A heavy wood-veneer door leading back out to the main facility corridor.
It has been bolted shut from the outside. The deadbolts are engaged.
There is no way back. You are supposed to be here.
A reverse-oriented peephole. It's designed so people outside can look in, not the other way around.
Looking through it backwards reveals a tiny, distorted fish-eye view of an empty hallway.
The hallway lights just flickered off. It is completely dark out there now.
An analog waveform monitor attached to the Harmonic Apparatus.
The green phosphor trace is flatlining. It needs an input signal.
A sticky note on the side reads: 'DO NOT EXCEED 400Hz UNDER ANY CIRCUMSTANCES'.
A monochrome cathode-ray tube display built directly into the vault casing.
The screen is burned-in with the words: 'SYSTEM LOCK. AWAITING CRYSTAL NODE'.
Touching the glass gives you a sharp static shock that tastes like copper.
A massive industrial lock wheel securing the blast door.
It is governed by the room's main terminal. Manual rotation is impossible.
The steel is cold. It hasn't been turned in years.

prop_facility_directory.flavorText: Institutional Clinical Personnel Ledger and Shift Roster. A hardboard clipboard mounted to the smoked teak board holds the shift schedules, inspection walkthrough logs, and confidential field notes for the 5 sanatorium duty staff.

prop_pneumatic_terminal.flavorText: Pneumatic Dispatch Terminal Model 72. High-speed vacuum conduit routing specimen tubes and patient intake dossiers to peripheral wings.

prop_waiting_bench.flavorText: A low institutional waiting bench constructed from bent teak and tubular chrome. The foam padding has hardened with age.

prop_wall_clock.flavorText: A synchronized master-slave wall clock. Its sweep-second hand clicks once every thirty seconds with a hollow mechanical shudder.
